processed.title: Human cognitive performance-associated gut microbiota influences learning and memory in mice through arginine and pterin metabolism.

figures.label: Figure 1.
figures.caption: (a) Schematic of Imageomics cohort analysis. (b) Human imageomics cohort Volcano plots showing up and down-regulation associated with SDMT after correcting for donor age, BMI, and years of education. Over representation analysis. Plots showing which microbiota are enriched and downregulated in association to human SDMT score. (c) Volcano plots of differential microbial molecular functions associated with SDMT in the human Aging Imageomics cohort (Significant associated genes were identified using the ANCOM-BC from shotgun metagenomics data, controlling for age, sex, BMI, and years of education. The log2 fold change of the association with a unit change in the ANCOM-BC-transformed variable values and the log10 p-values adjusted for multiple comparisons using a sequential goodness-of-fit were plotted for each taxon. Significance was set at p adj < 0.05. Significantly different genes are colored in green (upregulated) or red (downregulated). (d) Bar plots of the over-representation KEGG pathway analyzes (q-value < 0.1) mapping the KEGG orthologues significantly associated with SDMT in the human Aging Imageomics cohort. (e) Corresponding C-net plot of the arginine and proline pathway and ABC transporters showing significantly altered KEGG orthologues (f) Schematic representation of microbial metabolic pathways associated with SDMT scores, including creatinine/sarcosine metabolism and corresponding KEGG orthologues. (g) Bar plots of the over-representation functional KEGG modules (q-value < 0.1) significantly associated with SDMT in the human Aging Imageomics cohort.

figures.label: Figure 2.
figures.caption: (a) Schematic of the study design. Fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) was performed in mice using stool from human donors with high and low SDMT cognitive scores. Following the FMT period, mice underwent behavioral testing and omics profiling. Morris Water maze (MWM) tests showing: Time to platform; Path efficiency; Corrected Integrated Path Length (CIPL). (b) Data analyzed by stratifying recipient mice into high and low SDMT cognition groups based on the median SDMT score of the human cohort, using a mixed linear model with the interaction between test day and donor SDMT scores. Lines show model-estimated means (shaded 95% confidence intervals). Pairwise post-hoc are annotated * p < 0.05. (c) Representative Nissl staining of the cortex and CA1 region of the hippocampus in recipient mice, showing the relationship between human donor SDMT scores and neuronal density in recipient mice. Each point represents one human donor, with neuronal density calculated as the mean across recipient mice receiving FMT from that donor. Scale bar represents 200 μm. Corresponding Spearman correlations are displayed.

figures.label: Figure 3.
figures.caption: Metagenomics analysis of the microbiota and metabolomics of the hippocampus showing data associated with SDMT in the mouse recipients receiving FMT from the selected 13 human donors. All analyzes were controlled for age, BMI, and years of education. (a) Volcano plots of differentially abundant microbial species identified using the ANCOM-BC from shotgun metagenomics. The log2 fold change of the association with a unit change in the ANCOM-BC-transformed variable values and the log10 p-values adjusted for multiple comparisons using a sequential goodness-of-fit were plotted for each taxon. Significance was set at P adj < 0.1. Significantly different phyla are colored accordingly. (b) Bar plots of the over-representation KEGG pathway analyzes (q value < 0.1) mapping the KEGG orthologues significantly associated with donor SDMT scores. (c) C-net plot of differential microbial genes of the arginine and proline metabolic pathway following over-representation KEGG pathway analyzes (q value < 0.1) mapping the KEGG orthologues to determine overexpressed metabolic pathways. (d) Volcano plots of differential hippocampal metabolites identified applying a linear model to the data using the R package “limma” on metabolites identified by CIL-LC-MS. Significance was set at p adj < 0.1. Significantly different metabolite classes are colored accordingly. (e) Over-representation analysis using the metabolites associated with donor SDMT scores, identified with limma. Dots are colored according to the q-value. (f) C-net plot of differential metabolic pathways of the arginine biosynthesis, arginine and proline, tyrosine and folate metabolic pathways (q value < 0.1). (g) Schematic representation of metagenomic and metabolic pathways centered around the co-factor BH4, neurotransmitter synthesis and metabolic pathways associated with SDMT scores. For recipient mice, upregulated metabolites are colored in blue, while downregulated metabolites are shown in red. Differentially abundant KEGG orthologues are colored in green for humans and purple for recipient mice.

figures.label: Figure 4.
figures.caption: RNA-seq of the cortex in recipient mice controlled for age, BMI, and years of education. (a) Volcano plots of mPFC transcripts associated with donor SDMT following limma-voom analysis and correction for multiple comparisons. Genes of the dopaminergic synapse are labeled. (b) Bar plots of the over-representation RNA-seq pathway analyzes (q-value < 0.1) for genes significantly associated with donor SDMT. (c) Corresponding C-net plot of overexpressed pathways and genes corresponding to the Dopaminergic synapse and neuroactive ligand. (d) Schematic representation of gene alterations in the dopaminergic synapse where genes enriched are shown in blue and those downregulated are shown in red.

processed.title: Integrated multi-omics analysis reveals distinct metabolic signatures and gut microbiome alterations across the pediatric obesity spectrum.

figures.label: Figure 1.
figures.caption: Liver enzyme profiles in serum across pediatric weight categories. (A) Alanine aminotransferase (ALT); (B) aspartate aminotransferase (AST); (C) gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT). Scatter plots showing serum enzyme concentrations (U/L) in normal weight (NW, n = 16, yellow‒green circles), overweight (Ow, n = 12, dark blue circles), and obese (Ob, n = 20, pink circles) children and adolescents. Individual data points are presented with horizontal bars representing mean ± standard deviation. Statistical comparisons using ANOVA with post-hoc testing revealed a significant overall difference between normal weight and obese groups, indicated by one asterisk (* p < 0.05) or three asterisks (*** p < 0.001).

figures.label: Figure 2.
figures.caption: Alterations in fecal and serum metabolite profiles across the pediatric obesity spectrum. (A) Venn diagram showing distribution of significantly altered fecal metabolites in three pairwise comparisons: obese versus normal weight (Ob vs NW; pink circle, 126 unique metabolites, 35.9%), obese versus overweight (Ob vs Ow; blue circle, 143 unique metabolites, 40.7%) and overweight versus normal weight (Ow vs NW; purple circle, 12 unique metabolites, 3.4%). (B) Three-circle Venn diagram for serum metabolites across all three pairwise comparisons: Ob vs NW (top left, pink/red, 11 unique, 11.6%), Ob vs Ow (top right, blue, 52 unique, 54.7%), and overweight versus normal weight (Ow vs NW; bottom, purple, 15 unique, 15.8%). Intersection sizes are drawn proportionally. (C) Bubble dot plot displaying the top 20 significantly altered fecal metabolites for each comparison (panels: Ob vs NW, Ob vs Ow, Ow vs NW). The x-axis indicates direction of regulation (left = downregulated, right = upregulated). Each metabolite (y-axis) is shown as a circle; color represents adjusted p- value (yellow ≈ 0.03, orange ≈ 0.02, purple/dark ≤ 0.01), and circle size reflects absolute fold change (1- to 4-fold; larger circles = greater change). (D) Bubble dot plot for the top 20 significantly altered serum metabolites, arranged similarly. Bubble color follows a gradient from yellow ( p = 0.04) to dark purple/black ( p ≤ 0.01), with darker hues indicating higher significance. Bubble size corresponds to absolute fold change (scale: 2, 4, 6, 8). Together, these figures reveal progressive alterations in amino acid metabolism, redox homeostasis, and nucleotide biosynthesis pathways across the pediatric obesity spectrum.

figures.label: Figure 3.
figures.caption: Metabolic pathway enrichment analysis of fecal metabolites. (A) Obese versus normal weight children with focus on folate biosynthesis. (B) Obese versus overweight children with focus on pyrimidine metabolism. Left panel: pathway enrichment scatter plot displaying significantly altered metabolic pathways in fecal samples from obese (Ob) versus normal weight (NW) children. The x-axis represents pathway impact (0.0–1.0), calculated as the cumulative percentage of matched metabolites relative to total metabolites in each pathway. The y-axis shows statistical significance as −log₁₀( p-value). Each circle represents a distinct metabolic pathway, with circle size proportional to the number of significantly altered metabolites within that pathway and color intensity indicating statistical significance (red = highest significance, p < 0.01; orange = moderate significance, p < 0.05; yellow = lower significance, p < 0.10). Right panel: KEGG metabolic network diagram for the folate biosynthesis pathway, illustrating the biochemical relationships between significantly altered compounds. Rectangular nodes represent individual metabolites identified by KEGG compound identifiers (C-numbers), with node colors indicating differential abundance status: red = significantly downregulated in obesity ( p < 0.05, fold change > 1.5); yellow = moderately altered; light blue = not significantly altered.

figures.label: Figure 4.
figures.caption: Differentially abundant microbial taxa. Heatmap showing log2 fold changes of differentially abundant genera in three pairwise comparisons. Key depleted taxa in obesity include Faecalibacterium, Roseburia, Agathobacter, Bacteroides fragilis, and Akkermansia. Enriched taxa include Blautia, Dorea, Ruminococcus gnavus, Collinsella, and Escherichia-Shigella.

figures.label: Figure 5.
figures.caption: Metabolic pathway enrichment analysis of serum metabolites. (A) Obese- versus normal-weight children with a focus on beta-alanine metabolism. (B) Overweight versus normal-weight children with a focus on aromatic amino acid biosynthesis. Left panel: pathway enrichment scatter plot displaying significantly altered metabolic pathways in fecal samples from obese (Ob) versus normal-weight (NW) children. The x-axis represents pathway impact (0.0–1.0), calculated as the cumulative percentage of matched metabolites relative to total metabolites in each pathway. The y-axis shows statistical significance as −log₁₀( p-value). Each circle represents a distinct metabolic pathway, with circle size proportional to the number of significantly altered metabolites within that pathway and color intensity indicating statistical significance (red = highest significance, p < 0.01; orange = moderate significance, p < 0.05; yellow = lower significance, p < 0.10). Right panel: KEGG metabolic network diagram for the folate biosynthesis pathway, illustrating the biochemical relationships between significantly altered compounds. Rectangular nodes represent individual metabolites identified by KEGG compound identifiers (C-numbers), with node colors indicating differential abundance status: red = significantly downregulated in obesity ( p < 0.05, fold change > 1.5); yellow = moderately altered; light blue = not significantly altered.

figures.label: Figure 6.
figures.caption: Microbiome‒metabolite correlation heatmap. Heatmap showing Spearman correlations between differentially abundant genera and key metabolites, separately for NW and Ob groups. Strong positive correlations between beneficial bacteria (Faecalibacterium, Roseburia, Bacteroides, Akkermansia) and their characteristic metabolites (butyrate, propionate, bile acids) are present in NW but lost in Ob. Novel correlations between opportunistic taxa and pro- inflammatory metabolites emerge in Ob.

figures.label: Figure 7.
figures.caption: Diversity analysis of gut microbiota across BMI groups. (A) Box-and-whisker plot with individual data points overlaid, depicting alpha diversity of gut microbiota as measured by the Shannon diversity index across three weight status groups: normal weight (yellow-green, n = 12), overweight (dark blue, n = 6), and obese (pink, n = 38). The y-axis represents the Shannon diversity index (range: 3.5–5.5), a measure of both species richness and evenness within individual samples. The box spans the interquartile range (IQR; 25th–75th percentile), the horizontal line within each box denotes the median, and whiskers extend to 1.5 × the IQR. Individual sample values are overlaid as colored dots. Statistical comparisons between all group pairs were performed and annotated: normal weight vs. overweight (ns), overweight vs. obese (ns), and normal weight vs. obese (ns, spanning bracket). We found no significant differences in Shannon diversity across BMI groups. (B) Principal coordinate analysis (PCoA) ordination plot illustrating beta diversity dispersion of gut microbial communities across three weight status groups: normal weight (open black circles with black convex hulls), overweight (open green triangles with green convex hull), and obese (open red triangles with red convex hull). Distances between samples were calculated using Euclidean distance on centered log-ratio (CLR)-transformed abundance data. The x-axis (PCoA 1) and y-axis (PCoA 2) represent the first two principal coordinates capturing the major axes of variation in community composition. Convex hulls enclose the full range of each group's sample distribution, with gray lines connecting each sample to its group centroid label.

figures.label: Figure 8.
figures.caption: Differentially abundant microbial taxa in obese vs. overweight children (top 50 by p-value). Horizontal bar chart displaying the top 50 significantly differentially abundant microbial taxa (ranked by p-value) in the comparison of obese vs. overweight children. Microbial taxa are annotated following the hierarchical nomenclature of family–genus–species as provided by the sequencing core; in cases where complete taxonomic resolution was unavailable, partial annotations are shown. The x-axis represents the log₂ fold change (log₂FC), with positive values (rightward bars, light blue) indicating taxa upregulated in the Obese group relative to Overweight, and negative values (leftward bars, dark blue/purple) indicating downregulated taxa.

figures.label: Figure 9.
figures.caption: Relative abundance of differentially abundant microbes across BMI group comparisons. (A) Family level. Stacked bar chart depicting the relative abundance (%) of significantly differentially abundant microbial taxa at the family level across three pairwise BMI group comparisons: overweight vs. normal weight, obese vs. normal weight, and obese vs. overweight. Each bar represents the composite relative abundance of all differentially abundant families identified in that comparison, normalized to 100%. Individual families are color-coded according to the legend, which includes 30 distinct families spanning the major gut microbial phyla. (B) Genus level. Stacked bar chart illustrating the relative abundance (%) of significantly differentially abundant microbial taxa at the genus level across three pairwise BMI group comparisons: overweight vs. normal weight, obese vs. normal weight, and obese vs. overweight. Each bar represents the normalized composite relative abundance of all differentially abundant genera in that comparison, summing to 100%. Over 45 distinct genera are represented in the color-coded legend, encompassing major gut commensals and opportunistic taxa.

figures.label: Figure 10.
figures.caption: Genus–metabolite correlation heatmaps across weight status groups (overweight vs. normal weight and obesity vs. normal weight). (A) Spearman correlation heatmap for overweight vs. normal weight comparison showing 14 genera and 20 metabolites with |ρ| ≥ 0.60 (annotated values; * p < 0.05). Key positive associations include Alistipes with 1-aminocyclopropane-1-carboxylate ( ρ = 0.92), Lachnospiraceae_UCG-004 with acetate ( ρ = 0.90), and CAG-352 with L-pipecoline ( ρ = 0.92). Notable negative correlations include Lachnoclostridium with L-kynurenine ( ρ = −0.90) and GCA-900066575 with 1-aminocyclopropane-1-carboxylate ( ρ = −0.89). (B) Spearman genus–metabolite correlation heatmap for obesity vs. normal weight showing 18 genera and 22 metabolites prioritized by |ρ| ≥ 0.45. Elusimicrobium shows positive correlations with 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutarate ( ρ = 0.49) and propionate ( ρ = 0.49), while UCG_002 exhibits negative correlations with 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutarate ( ρ = −0.64) and propionate ( ρ = −0.64). Blue = negative correlation; red = positive correlation.

figures.label: Figure 11.
figures.caption: Genus–metabolite correlation heatmaps in the overweight subgroup and differential correlation analysis (overweight minus obesity). (A) Spearman correlation heatmap for overweight participants ( n = 5) showing 18 genera and 20 metabolites. Strong associations (|ρ| = 1.00) are observed between Catenibacterium and 1-methylhistidine ( ρ = −1.00), Fusicatenibacter and 6-aminonicotinic acid ( ρ = 1.00), and Rikenellaceae RC9 gut group with glycine and histidine ( ρ = 1.00). (B) Spearman correlation heatmap for obese participants ( n = 31) showing attenuated correlations relative to the overweight subgroup; Parabacteroides with N-acetylspermidine ( ρ = 0.71) and Bacteroides ( ρ = 0.64) are among the most prominent associations. (C) Differential correlation heatmap (Δρ = overweight minus obesity) highlighting the most divergent genus–metabolite relationships between weight categories. The largest positive differential is Catenibacterium–Salicinol (Δρ = 1.88) and the largest negative differential is Catenibacterium–1-methylhistidine (Δρ = −1.68), underscoring weight-status-specific microbiome–metabolome coupling. Blue = overweight < obesity; red = overweight > obesity.

processed.title: Urinary ubiquitin-specific protease 2 (USP2) as a diagnostic biomarker for chronic kidney disease: an integrated multi-omics and network analysis.

figures.label: Figure 1.
figures.caption: Association between urinary ubiquitin-specific protease 2 (USP2) and chronic kidney disease (CKD), and diagnostic performance of USP2-based models. (A) Forest plot showing univariate and multivariate Firth logistic regression results for age, sex, and urinary USP2. The multivariate model included age, sex, and USP2. (B) Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves for USP2, USP2 + Age, USP2 + Sex, and USP2 + Age + Sex. (C) Decision curve analysis (DCA) for the same USP2-based models. Dashed curves indicate treat-all and treat-none strategies. Data are presented as odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). OR, odds ratio; CI, confidence interval; ROC, receiver operating characteristic; AUC, area under the curve; DCA, decision curve analysis.

figures.label: Figure 2.
figures.caption: Urinary and serum metabolomics analyses. Panels A–F show urinary metabolomics results comparing CKD urine samples (UCKD) with healthy-control urine samples (UN): (A) OPLS-DA score plot; (B) permutation testing; (C) metabolite chemical classification; (D) volcano plot with metabolites classified as FDR < 0.05, raw P < 0.05 only, or not significant; (E) VIP-ranked metabolites; and (F) pathway enrichment. Panels G–L show serum metabolomics results comparing CKD serum samples (SCKD) with healthy-control serum samples (SN): (G) OPLS-DA score plot; (H) permutation testing; (I) metabolite chemical classification; (J) volcano plot with metabolites classified as FDR < 0.05, raw P < 0.05 only, or not significant; (K) VIP-ranked metabolites; and (L) pathway enrichment. OPLS-DA, orthogonal partial least-squares discriminant analysis; VIP, variable importance in projection; FDR, false discovery rate; UCKD, urine samples from patients with CKD; UN, urine samples from healthy controls; SCKD, serum samples from patients with CKD; SN, serum samples from healthy controls.

figures.label: Figure 3.
figures.caption: Weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) of urinary and serum metabolites. Panels A–C show urinary metabolite WGCNA: (A) Scale-free topology fit index (R2) and mean connectivity across candidate soft-thresholding powers. (B) Metabolite clustering dendrogram and module assignment. (C) Module-trait heatmap showing Pearson correlation coefficients, nominal P values, and FDR-adjusted P values for age, sex, urinary USP2, and CKD. Panels D–F show serum metabolite WGCNA: (D) Scale-free topology fit index (R2) and mean connectivity across candidate soft-thresholding powers. (E) Metabolite clustering dendrogram and module assignment. (F) Module-trait heatmap showing Pearson correlation coefficients, nominal P values, and FDR-adjusted P values for age, sex, urinary USP2, and CKD. FDR values were calculated within each module-trait heatmap. WGCNA, weighted gene co-expression network analysis; USP2, ubiquitin-specific protease 2; CKD, chronic kidney disease.

figures.label: Figure 4.
figures.caption: Identification of urinary metabolite candidates mediating the association between urinary USP2 and CKD. (A) Bubble plot showing urinary metabolites from the WGCNA module selected according to their correlations with CKD and urinary USP2. Bubble size and color intensity represent the magnitude of correlation; the signs of the correlations are indicated by the plotted values. (B–H) Mediation analyses illustrating the indirect effects of 6-gingerol, gly-met-lys, deoxycholic acid 3-glucuronide, N-(3-acetamido-2-oxochromen-6-yl)-4-nitrobenzamide, 1,2-dihydronaphthalene-1,2-diol, N-benzyl-4-benzylsulfonylbutanamide, and 16-ketoestradiol on the association between urinary USP2 and CKD. Each triangular diagram represents a mediation model, including the total effect (top), direct effect (left), and indirect effect (right). Mediation proportions are indicated within each panel. All mediation models were adjusted for age and sex. Regression coefficients are presented with corresponding P values. The mediation proportion was calculated as the ratio of the indirect effect to the total effect.

figures.label: Figure 5.
figures.caption: WGCNA of plasma proteomics. (A) Scale-free topology fit index (R2) and mean connectivity across candidate soft-thresholding powers. (B) Protein clustering dendrogram and module assignment. (C) Module-trait heatmap showing Pearson correlation coefficients, nominal P values, and FDR-adjusted P values for age, sex, urinary USP2, and CKD. The turquoise and greenyellow modules were significantly associated with age, urinary USP2, and CKD after FDR adjustment. The purple module was significantly associated with urinary USP2 and CKD, whereas its correlation with age was nominal but not FDR-significant. WGCNA, weighted gene co-expression network analysis; FDR, false discovery rate.

figures.label: Figure 6.
figures.caption: Identification of serum metabolite candidates whose association with CKD is mediated by urinary USP2. (A) Bubble plot showing the 12 serum metabolites selected from the WGCNA turquoise module according to their correlations with CKD and urinary USP2. Bubble size and color intensity represent the magnitude of correlation; the signs of the correlations are indicated by the plotted values. (B–M) Mediation analyses testing whether urinary USP2 mediates the association between the 12 serum metabolites and CKD. Each triangular diagram represents a mediation model, including the total effect (top), direct effect (left), and indirect effect (right). Mediation proportions are indicated within each panel. All mediation models were adjusted for age and sex. Regression coefficients are presented with corresponding P values. The mediation proportion was calculated as the ratio of the indirect effect to the total effect.

figures.label: Figure 7.
figures.caption: Identification of plasma proteins associated with urinary USP2 and CKD across WGCNA modules. (A–C) Bubble plots showing representative plasma proteins from three WGCNA modules (purple, turquoise, and greenyellow) that were strongly correlated with both CKD and urinary USP2. Bubble size and color intensity represent the absolute value of the correlation coefficient. Proteins in the purple and turquoise modules showed consistent positive correlations with both CKD and urinary USP2, whereas proteins in the greenyellow module showed consistent negative correlations. The turquoise module displays the top 20 proteins ranked by the product of the correlation coefficients with CKD and USP2. All proteins were quantified from plasma samples.
